slides.heading: Bst Construction
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Medium · Binary Search Trees
slides.narration: Let's solve Bst Construction, a medium binary search trees problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: A BST class supporting insert, contains and remove (duplicates go right; removing a node with two children replaces it with its in-order successor's value).
Removing the only node is a no-op.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. A BST class supporting insert, contains and remove (duplicates go right; removing a node with two children replaces it with its in-order successor's value). Removing the only node is a no-op.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Insert, search and remove all follow the BST ordering; removal of a two-child node swaps in the smallest value of the right subtree.
slides.narration: Insert, search and remove all follow the BST ordering; removal of a two-child node swaps in the smallest value of the right subtree.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Unbalanced BST ops: O(h) — O(log n) average, O(n) worst
Alternative: sorted array → O(log n) search but O(n) insert
Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) guarantee O(log n)
slides.narration: A sorted array gives fast search but slow inserts. A BST makes insert, search and remove all proportional to the height: log n on average, but linear if the tree degenerates. Self-balancing trees guarantee log n.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Walk left or right by comparison
3. To remove with two children, copy the right subtree's minimum and delete it there
slides.narration: Step by step. First, walk left or right by comparison. Second, insert at the empty spot. Third, to remove with two children, copy the right subtree's minimum and delete it there. Fourth, handle the root carefully.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Start: BST built from 10, 5, 15, 2, 5, 13, 22, 1
slides.narration: Here's a BST built by inserting ten, five, fifteen, two, five, thirteen, twenty-two and one. Equal values go right.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: insert(14): at 10 → go right
slides.narration: To insert fourteen, compare with 10: fourteen is larger, so go right.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: insert(14): at 15 → go left
slides.narration: To insert fourteen, compare with 15: fourteen is smaller, so go left.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: insert(14): at 13 → go right
slides.narration: To insert fourteen, compare with 13: fourteen is larger, so go right.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 14 becomes 13's right child
slides.narration: Thirteen has no right child, so fourteen goes there.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: remove(10): two children → copy min of right subtree (13)
slides.narration: Removing the root, ten, which has two children: copy the smallest value of its right subtree, thirteen, into the root, then remove thirteen from the right subtree, where it has at most one child.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Result: 13 at the root; 14 moves up
slides.narration: The result: thirteen at the root, and fourteen takes thirteen's old place.

slides.heading: Java solution (1/2)
slides.narration: Insert walks down comparing values, going left for smaller and right otherwise, and attaches a new node at the first empty spot. Contains walks the same way and returns true on equality.

slides.heading: Java solution (2/2)
slides.narration: Remove finds the node while tracking its parent. With two children, it copies the right subtree's minimum and removes that. With one child, it splices the child in, handling the root specially by copying the child's value and pointers.

slides.heading: Complexity
bullets: Time: O(log n) avg, O(n) worst per op
slides.narration: Time is O of log n avg, O of n worst per op. Space is constant (iterative).

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Remove the root when it has one child (no parent to relink)
Equal values go right — be consistent
Remove a value that doesn't exist → no-op
slides.narration: The nastiest case is removing the root when it has only one child, since there's no parent to relink. Be consistent that equal values go right.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Follow-up: make it self-balancing; add size for rank queries
slides.narration: Iterative versions avoid recursion overhead. Follow-ups include balancing and augmenting nodes with subtree sizes.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Insert, search and remove all follow the BST ordering; removal of a two-child node swaps in the smallest value of the right subtree.
Complexity: O(log n) avg, O(n) worst per op
slides.narration: To recap Bst Construction: Insert, search and remove all follow the BST ordering; removal of a two-child node swaps in the smallest value of the right subtree. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
